lessons.culture: Moroccans often share food from one plate and say "بسم الله" before starting and "الحمد لله" after. Mint tea (أتاي) is offered almost everywhere, and refusing it outright can seem cold, so a guest usually accepts at least one glass. Falafel is not a traditional Moroccan dish (people more often eat tajine, couscous or harira), but it is sold as a street snack in some cities.

lessons.culture: A traditional Moroccan "دار" is built around an inner courtyard with a main salon for guests, while many city families now live in a "شقة". A guest praises a house with "ما شاء الله" and the host answers "الله يخليك"; the roof "السطح" is used for drying washing and for sitting out on summer evenings.

lessons.culture: In a Moroccan home guests are taken straight to the salon near the entrance and served mint tea. "بيت الما" is the bathroom or toilet (also called "الطواليط"), often a small separate room, and the flat roof "السطح" is a normal part of the house.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "فين الكوزينة؟" Say it is next to the living room.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "حدا الصالون".

exercises.tip: "حدا" means next to.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "فين بيت الما؟" Say in the corridor, on the right.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "فالكوريدور على اليمين".

exercises.tip: "كوريدور" comes from French and is the everyday word.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "إيه، واجد".

exercises.tip: "بيت" is masculine in this phrase, so "واجد".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "بيوت النعاس _____." Meaning: The bedrooms are upstairs.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "تحت".

exercises.tip: "تحت" is down or below.

lessons.culture: Most Moroccan kitchens cook on a butane gas cooker ("بوطاغاز") fed from a gas bottle. Many household objects keep their French names in speech, such as "تيليكوموند" (remote control) and "لامبة" (lamp), and in winter people pile on heavy blankets because many homes have no central heating.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "فين التيليكوموند؟" Say it is on the table.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "فوق الطبلة".

exercises.tip: "فوق" is on or above.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "شنو خاصك؟" Say you need a blanket.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "خاصني بطانية".

exercises.tip: "خاصني" is "I need" and is followed straight by the thing.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "واش الغسالة كتخدم؟" Say no, it does not work.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "لا، ما كتخدمش".

exercises.tip: "خدم" is both to work (a job) and to work (a machine).

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "حل الطاقة".

exercises.tip: "حل" is the everyday word for open.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The mirror is next to the door."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "المراية حدا الباب".

exercises.tip: "مراية" is a mirror.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "fan"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "مروحة".

exercises.tip: "مروحة" is a fan; "لامبة" is a lamp.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Moroccan speech says "تيليكوموند".

exercises.tip: "تيليكوموند" comes from French.

exercises.tip: "ما" before the verb and "ش" after it make it negative.

challenge.title: Meeting Family Over a Meal
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Moroccan Arabic conversation of at least 10 lines. It must ask about someone's family, describe a relative, say you are hungry or thirsty, order food or drink, use the exchange بالهنا والشفا / الله يبارك فيك or صحة / الله يعطيك الصحة, and ask for the bill. Use at least 8 phrases from Unit 2, with a masculine and a feminine address form.
required_elements: A question about family using واش عندك عائلة? or شحال ديال الناس فعائلتك?
A relative described using ماما, بابا, خويا, ختي, راجلي, مراتي, ولدي or بنتي.
Hunger or thirst using جيعان, جيعانة or عطشان.
An order or wish for food or drink using بغيت ناكل or بغيت نشرب.
The exchange بالهنا والشفا / الله يبارك فيك, or صحة / الله يعطيك الصحة.
A request for the bill using الحساب عافاك or شحال الحساب?
Both a masculine form (واش نتا) and a feminine form (واش نتي).
